lines.text: Here's an experiment that still messes with my head.
Shine light through one narrow slit, and the wall behind it lights up.
Open a second slit next to it, and parts of the wall get darker.
Let's model light as a wave: crests in red, troughs in blue, spreading out from the slit.
Add the second slit, and the two sets of ripples overlap.
But look at these grey lines. Along them, the wave barely moves.
Freeze time and pick a point on one. It's exactly half a wavelength farther from one slit than the other.
So a crest from one always meets a trough from the other, and they cancel.
Here, the difference is one whole wavelength. Crest meets crest, and the wave is twice as tall.
Average over time, and you get bands. Bright, dark, bright.
Plot the brightness on the wall: the dark spots are dimmer than one slit alone.
Now the twist. Send light through one photon at a time, and each lands at a single point.
Yet after thousands of them, the same dark bands appear.
So even one photon's landing spot depends on both slits being open.
